about.title: Putting It Together: Your Home Plan Checklist
about.length_note: About 8 minutes. It is 16 short beats, and you can stop after any one of them. The checklist is meant to be filled in over days or weeks, not in one sitting.

sources.title: Prepare Your Health: Power Outages (CDC fact sheet)
sources.publisher: Centers for Disease Control and Prevention

sources.title: Emergency Power Planning for People Who Use Electricity and Battery-Dependent Assistive Technology and Medical Devices

say.text: Welcome to the last class. Today you will build a one-page checklist and set a date to look at it again.

show.text: Putting It Together: Your Home Plan Checklist

say.text: First, a kind note. Doing a little is better than doing nothing. Go at your own pace, and stop whenever you need to.

show.text: A little is better than nothing

say.text: Your checklist has three boxes: Done, Next, and Later. Every item from this course goes in one of them.

ask.q: Sam already made a 911 card and put it by the phone. Which box does it go in?
wrong: It does not go on the checklist
ask.why: The Done box holds what you have already finished. It is good to see it there.

say.text: Group one is reaching help. It covers the 911 call, texting 911, the 911 card by the phone, and the one-page medical sheet.

show.text: Calling 911; Texting 911 where offered; 911 card by the phone; One-page medical sheet for the ER

say.text: Call if you can, text if you can't. A voice call gives the call-takers more information. Whether texting works depends on your local 911 center.

show.text: Call if you can, text if you can't

ask.right: Each local 911 center decides whether it accepts texts, so check with yours. Where texts are not accepted, you get an automatic reply telling you to call.
wrong: It works the same everywhere in the country.
It is always better than calling.
You do not need to check anything before an emergency.
ask.why: The FCC says each call center decides whether to accept texts. Where it is not available, the carrier sends a bounce-back message.

say.text: If you do text, send your location and what is wrong, in plain words. Do not send photos, and do not add other people to the text.

show.text: Location first; What is wrong, in plain words; Complete words, not short-hand; No photos, videos or emojis; Not a group text

ask.q: What belongs in a text to 911?
ask.right: Your address and what is wrong, in plain words
wrong: A group text that includes your family
ask.why: The 911 center may not know your location when you text. Photos, videos, emojis and group texts are not supported or may not arrive.

say.text: Group two is fire. Tell your local fire department, on its non-emergency number, that someone with a disability lives at your address.

ask.q: Which number do you use to tell the fire department about your needs ahead of time?
wrong: The first number you find online
ask.why: The U.S. Fire Administration checklist says to use the non-emergency line. The fire department may also help with your escape plan and a home safety check.

say.text: Next, alarms and drills. Test smoke alarms at least once a month. Practice your escape plan at least twice a year.

show.text: Test smoke alarms monthly; Replace them every 10 years; Practice the escape plan twice a year, including for someone who cannot walk

ask.q: How often should you test smoke alarms?
ask.why: NFPA says to test all smoke alarms at least once a month. The 10 years is how long an alarm lasts before you replace it.

say.text: Group three is power. If someone uses electric medical equipment, plan for a power cut before it happens.

show.text: Make an emergency power plan; Check if the device can run on batteries or a generator; Tell the fire department and the power and water companies

say.text: Ask your electric company about a priority list or medical registry. Even so, keep your own backup. A registry does not promise power.

show.text: Registry: you tell the company about your needs. Backup: you still plan your own batteries or other power.

ask.q: Sam has told the electric company about a medical device. What else should Sam do?
ask.right: Still have a backup power plan
wrong: Wait for the next outage to decide
ask.why: One power company says a medical certificate does not guarantee uninterrupted power. You still need your own backup plan.

say.text: Group four is your go-bag and medicine supply. Ready.gov says to rethink your needs every year and update the kit as they change.

show.text: Go-bag packed; Medication supply on hand; Medical sheet copy inside; Update when needs change

ask.right: Needs change, so what is in it should change too
wrong: Because bags wear out every month
It only needs updating after an emergency
ask.why: Ready.gov says to rethink your needs each year and update the kit as your family's needs change.

say.text: Group five is weather. In a winter storm, a home may lose heat, power and phone service, and supplies may run short. Plan for extreme heat too.

show.text: Winter storm plan: heat, power, phone, supplies; Extreme heat plan; Extra medicines on hand

say.text: Group six is your contact plan. Pick an out-of-town contact, save an In Case of Emergency number in each phone, and say who calls whom.

show.text: Out-of-town contact; In Case of Emergency (ICE) number in every phone; Who calls whom; Meeting places

ask.q: Why pick a contact who lives out of town?
ask.right: They may be easier to reach in a disaster
wrong: Because they can reach 911 for you
Because texts do not work locally
ask.why: Ready.gov suggests someone out of town, because they may be easier to reach in a disaster.

say.text: How often should you check each piece? Here is a quick look. Smoke alarms come up most often, so put them on a monthly reminder.

show.text: How often to check, times per year

ask.q: Which item on the chart is checked most often?
ask.why: NFPA says to test smoke alarms at least once a month, which is about 12 times a year.

say.text: Now pick the next two things for this week. Choose one quick job and one job that matters most for your person.

ask.q: Sam looks at the checklist and finds eight gaps. What does this class suggest?
ask.right: Pick two to do this week and leave the rest in Later
wrong: Try to do all eight tonight
Give up until everything is perfect
ask.why: Small steps count. Doing a little is better than doing nothing, and you can go at your own pace.

say.text: One of your next things can be booking a hands-on first-aid and CPR class. Both the Red Cross and the American Heart Association offer them.

show.text: Red Cross: classes take a few hours; AHA: hands-on skills session for the card; Card valid two years; Needs a class near you: use their Find a Class tools

ask.q: What does a hands-on class give you that reading a lesson cannot?
ask.right: Practice with an instructor who can watch your skills
wrong: A way to skip your doctor
ask.why: The Red Cross says an online class does not let you show your skills to an instructor. The AHA's card for CPR classes requires a hands-on skills session.

say.text: Last, set a review date. Write it on the checklist and tell one other person. On that day, move items from Next to Done and update anything that changed.

ask.q: What do you do on your review date?
ask.right: Look at the checklist, update what changed, and pick the next two things
ask.why: Ready.gov says to update your kit as needs change. It also says to review your family contact plan at least once a year or when information changes.

say.text: Two reminders. Check with your local 911 center or fire department, because services vary by place. Talk with the person's own doctors about their needs.

ask.q: Who should you ask whether a backup power source is right for a medical device?
ask.right: The device maker or supplier, and the person's own doctors
ask.why: The CDC says to read the manual or contact the manufacturer. This course does not replace first-aid training or the person's doctors.

say.text: You have done something kind and useful just by getting here. Fill in Done, Next and Later, set your date, and stop when you need to rest.

show.text: Done | Next (two things this week) | Later | Review date: ____ | Local 911 center and fire department checked | Doctors asked

charts.title: How often to check each part of your plan (times per year)

other_side.claim: A go-bag should be rethought about once a year.
other_side.other_view: Ready.gov says to rethink needs every year. One county emergency-services page says to check a kit at least twice a year so that nothing has expired. Both can work. This lesson suggests tying the check to a date you will remember, and doing it sooner if needs change.

other_side.claim: Take a hands-on class rather than only an online one.
other_side.other_view: The Red Cross says online-only classes do not let you show your skills to an instructor. The American Heart Association also offers fully self-directed online courses and a virtual hands-on session with an instructor. The best choice depends on your needs and what you can access. This course suggests an in-person or instructor-led skills session where you can get one.
